title: Dinah, Shechem, and the Sword
summary: Shechem violates Dinah, Jacob keeps silent, and Simeon and Levi turn the covenant sign into a trap and massacre the city.
historicalContext: Jacob has returned from Paddan-aram, crossed the Jordan, bought a field from the sons of Hamor, and raised an altar beside the city of Shechem (33:18-20). Shechem sat in the pass between Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim, an old and strategic settlement already known in Egyptian records, ruled here by Hamor, a Hivite chief. Some years have passed since the return, for Dinah, born after Leah’s six sons (30:21), is now a young woman and her brothers are grown men who tend the flocks. The family is still a seminomadic clan without citizenship, while the city is a settled community with its own council at the gate. The customs behind the chapter belong to that world: a bride-price paid to a young woman’s family, the father and brothers acting as her guardians, and circumcision practised by several ancient peoples, though for Abraham’s house it was the sign of God’s covenant (17:9-14).
literaryContext: The chapter interrupts the journey that should have taken Jacob to Bethel to keep his vow (28:20-22); only after the disaster does God send him there (35:1). It is built from two acts of violence with negotiations between them: Shechem’s assault on Dinah (vv. 1-4) and the brothers’ assault on the city (vv. 25-29), joined by speeches in which every party bargains and two parties deceive (vv. 5-24). Key words repeat: “defiled” (vv. 5, 13, 27), “took” (vv. 2, 4, 25-28), “went out” (vv. 1, 6, 24, 26), and “daughter” or “sister.” God is never named, and Dinah never speaks. The narrator lets Jacob’s silence and his sons’ fury stand side by side and gives the brothers the closing question, yet Jacob’s dying words in 49:5-7 supply the verdict on their anger. The episode also opens the account of how the elder sons forfeit leadership, as Reuben does in 35:22.
themes: Sexual violence named as folly in Israel
A father’s silence and a family’s fury
The covenant sign misused for revenge
Assimilation offered as a shortcut to the land
God’s protection of a failing family

outline.title: Dinah Violated
outline.summary: Dinah goes out to visit the women of the land, and Shechem the prince seizes and violates her, then asks his father to get her for his wife.

outline.title: Silence, Outrage, and Offers
outline.summary: Jacob keeps silent, his sons burn with anger at the folly done in Israel, and Hamor and Shechem offer intermarriage, land, and any bride-price.

outline.title: A Deceitful Bargain
outline.summary: Jacob’s sons answer with deceit, demanding circumcision of every male, and Hamor and Shechem persuade their city with the promise of Jacob’s wealth.

outline.title: Massacre and Plunder
outline.summary: On the third day Simeon and Levi kill the men of the city, take Dinah from Shechem’s house, and the brothers plunder flocks, wealth, women, and children.

outline.title: Fear and an Unanswered Question
outline.summary: Jacob rebukes Simeon and Levi out of fear of reprisal, and they answer with the question of how their sister had been treated.

verses.bibleText: And Dinah the daughter of Leah, which she bare unto Jacob, went out to see the daughters of the land.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The chapter opens with a young woman whose birth was noted in a single line (30:21) and who has not been mentioned since. Dinah is introduced as “the daughter of Leah, which she bare unto Jacob.” Naming the mother in this way is unusual and purposeful. It ties Dinah to her full brothers, Leah’s sons Simeon and Levi, who will take up her cause in verse 25, and it quietly recalls that Leah was the wife Jacob loved less (29:30-31). Every family tension of the earlier chapters stands behind this introduction.

Dinah “went out to see the daughters of the land.” The family had settled within sight of Shechem and bought a field there (33:18-19), so contact with the townspeople was close at hand. A young woman visiting other young women was an ordinary thing to do, and the text records no wrongdoing on her part. The phrase “daughters of the land” has a history in Genesis, though. It was Rebekah’s name for the Hittite women who grieved her and Isaac (27:46), and both Abraham and Isaac had kept their sons from marrying among the Canaanites (24:3; 28:1). The family’s calling to be distinct was already being tested by Jacob’s choice to settle beside a Canaanite city instead of going on to Bethel to fulfil his vow (28:20-22; 35:1).

The responsibility for what follows belongs to the man who commits the crime, and the narrator makes that clear in the next verse. Yet the setting is worth noticing. A household that had stopped short of God’s appointed place was living exposed, and its most vulnerable member paid the price. Jacob was the one charged with guarding his family, and he will be largely absent from the chapter until its end. Scripture often traces how a leader’s compromise leaves others unprotected (1 Samuel 2:22-25), and it calls those who lead households to watch over the weak (Psalm 82:3-4).

wordNotes.explanation: The ordinary verb for going out from a place. It is a key word in the chapter: Dinah goes out (v. 1), Hamor goes out to Jacob (v. 6), the men who go out of the city gate are circumcised (v. 24), and Simeon and Levi go out with Dinah after the slaughter (v. 26). The repetition traces the movement of the story from one going out to its violent reversal; the verb itself implies nothing improper about Dinah’s visit (compare Genesis 24:15).

wordNotes.term: לִרְאוֹת בִּבְנוֹת הָאָרֶץ (lir’ot bivnot ha’arets) — to see the daughters of the land
wordNotes.explanation: “To see” with the preposition be- can mean to visit or look upon with interest. “Daughters of the land” refers to the local Canaanite women, the same group Rebekah had dreaded as wives for her sons (Genesis 27:46). Dinah goes to see, but in the next verse she is seen; the verb links her visit to Shechem’s gaze without making her responsible for his act.

verses.bibleText: And when Shechem the son of Hamor the Hivite, prince of the country, saw her, he took her, and lay with her, and defiled her.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Shechem the son of Hamor the Hivite, prince of the country” bears the name of the city his family ruled. The Hivites appear in the table of nations among the descendants of Canaan (10:15-17), and Hamor is the man from whose sons Jacob had just bought his field (33:19). Shechem is a prince, accustomed to power and to having his wishes met. That status explains much of what follows: the ease with which he acts, the way he speaks to his father, and the town’s willingness to follow his lead.

The crime is told in four swift verbs: he “saw her,” he “took her,” he “lay with her,” and he “defiled her.” The sequence of seeing and taking recalls Genesis 6:2, where the powerful took whatever women they chose, and it echoes the pattern of Eve’s seeing and taking in 3:6. The Hebrew of “lay with her” uses a construction that makes Dinah the object of the act rather than a partner in it, and the final verb means to humble, afflict, or force. The same verb describes the rape of Tamar by Amnon (2 Samuel 13:14) and the violation of the Levite’s concubine (Judges 20:5). The text presents an act of force by a man with power against a young woman with none.

The narrator places the guilt on Shechem alone. Four verbs belong to him; Dinah is given none. The chapter will go on to speak of folly, defilement, and a thing that “ought not to be done” (v. 7), and Moses’ law would later treat the forcing of a woman as a grave crime (Deuteronomy 22:25-29). Readers should take care here. Those who have suffered sexual violence have sometimes been told, even in the church, that they invited it. Scripture does not say that of Dinah. The God who saw Hagar in her affliction and was named “Thou God seest me” (16:13) sees every Dinah. He is “nigh unto them that are of a broken heart” (Psalm 34:18), and Christ’s own ministry was marked by tenderness toward women whom others shamed or ignored (Luke 7:44-50).

Dinah’s voice is never heard in the chapter. She is spoken about, bargained over, and finally carried away, but never asked what she wants. That silence is part of the story’s honesty about how she was treated, and it invites readers to listen to those whom others pass over.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb ‘anah in this stem means to humble, afflict, or oppress. Genesis uses it of Sarai’s harsh treatment of Hagar (Genesis 16:6) and of Israel’s affliction in Egypt (Genesis 15:13). In sexual contexts it describes a man’s forcing or degrading of a woman, as with Amnon and Tamar (2 Samuel 13:14). The KJV’s “defiled” captures the shame placed upon her; the Hebrew stresses the violence and humiliation of the act.

A title for a leader or chief, one “lifted up” above others. Abraham was called a “mighty prince” by the Hittites (Genesis 23:6), and the word later names the tribal leaders of Israel (Numbers 7:2). Here it marks Shechem’s position and power, which make his act an abuse of strength against the defenceless.

verses.bibleText: And his soul clave unto Dinah the daughter of Jacob, and he loved the damsel, and spake kindly unto the damsel.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Three verbs of attachment follow the four verbs of violence. Shechem’s “soul clave unto Dinah,” he “loved the damsel,” and he “spake kindly unto the damsel.” The narrator records his feelings honestly but does not use them to soften the crime. The order matters: the assault is told first, the affection afterward. Whatever Shechem felt, it came after he had already taken what he wanted.

“Clave” is the word of Genesis 2:24, where a man leaves father and mother and cleaves to his wife. Shechem has inverted the order God gave. He forced the union first and only then sought the bond, and he never left his father’s house to do it; he will ask his father to arrange matters (v. 4). Even the love is shadowed. Elsewhere in Scripture a man’s desire after violating a woman can turn quickly to hatred (2 Samuel 13:15), and here it stays possessive, for Shechem keeps Dinah in his house throughout the negotiations (v. 26).

“Spake kindly” is literally “spoke to the heart.” The phrase is used of comforting or persuading words (50:21; Hosea 2:14). Shechem tries to win Dinah over after harming her. Kind words do not undo violence, though, and the chapter contains no confession, apology, or attempt to make things right with her family before he asks for her hand. Real repentance names the wrong and seeks to restore what was damaged (Luke 19:8). Shechem offers affection and, later, money, but never acknowledges what he has done.

wordNotes.term: וַתִּדְבַּק נַפְשׁוֹ (wattidbaq nafsho) — his soul clave
wordNotes.explanation: Davaq means to cling or stick fast. It describes a husband’s bond to his wife (Genesis 2:24), Ruth’s loyalty to Naomi (Ruth 1:14), and Israel’s call to hold fast to the Lord (Deuteronomy 10:20). Nefesh here means the whole self in its desires; the phrase describes strong attachment. In this setting it is a craving that followed an act of force, an attachment without the covenant faithfulness the word usually implies.

wordNotes.term: וַיְדַבֵּר עַל־לֵב הַנַּעֲרָ (wayedabber ‘al-lev hanna‘arah) — spake kindly unto the damsel
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “he spoke upon the heart of the young woman.” The idiom describes reassuring or wooing speech, used of Joseph comforting his brothers (Genesis 50:21) and of the Lord alluring Israel back (Hosea 2:14). The narrator calls Dinah na‘arah, a young woman of marriageable age, a term that preserves her dignity.

verses.bibleText: And Shechem spake unto his father Hamor, saying, Get me this damsel to wife.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Shechem’s request to his father is blunt: “Get me this damsel to wife.” There is no courtesy in it and no mention of what he has done. The verb translated “get” is the same verb rendered “took” in verse 2. He took her once by force and now asks his father to take her for him by arrangement. The tone is that of a young man used to having his wishes satisfied, much like Samson’s later demand to his parents (Judges 14:2).

He also speaks of Dinah differently from the narrator. Verse 3 called her “the damsel,” a young woman; here Shechem calls her “this girl,” using a word for a child. The shift exposes how he regards her, as something to be obtained. Marriage was indeed the remedy that later law provided when a man forced an unbetrothed woman, with a heavy payment and no right of divorce (Deuteronomy 22:28-29), and that law protected a woman who would otherwise be left without security. Even there, though, the father had the right to refuse (Exodus 22:16-17). Shechem goes about it in reverse, keeping her in his house and then sending his father to negotiate, so that Jacob’s family must bargain while Dinah is held.

Hamor responds at once to his son’s demand. The close cooperation of this Canaanite father and son stands in pointed contrast to the distance between Jacob and his own children in the verses that follow.

wordNotes.explanation: Yaldah is a girl or young female child, the feminine of yeled, “child.” It appears only a few times (Joel 3:3; Zechariah 8:5). The narrator has just called Dinah na‘arah, a young woman; Shechem’s choice of “this girl” is dismissive and impersonal, naming her as an object he wants rather than a person he has wronged.

verses.bibleText: And Jacob heard that he had defiled Dinah his daughter: now his sons were with his cattle in the field: and Jacob held his peace until they were come.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Jacob heard that he had defiled Dinah his daughter.” The narrator stresses the relationship: she is “his daughter.” What follows is startling. “Jacob held his peace until they were come.” Elsewhere Genesis records Jacob’s emotions vividly. He wept when he met Rachel (29:11), he was greatly afraid before Esau (32:7), and when he believed Joseph was dead he tore his clothes and refused comfort (37:34-35). At the news of Dinah’s violation the text records no grief, no anger, and no action, only silence.

Some caution is fair. Jacob was outnumbered, a resident alien beside a fortified town, with his sons away in the fields; waiting for them before deciding anything had a certain prudence. Proverbs praises the one who rules his spirit (Proverbs 16:32). Yet the story does not commend his silence. It sets his stillness against his sons’ grief and anger in verse 7, and it never shows Jacob speaking a word for Dinah, comforting her, or demanding her return. The pattern is painfully familiar. When Amnon violated Tamar, David “was very wroth” but did nothing, and his inaction opened the way for Absalom’s revenge (2 Samuel 13:21-29). A father’s passivity left room for his sons’ violence in both families.

The word “defiled” describes Dinah’s condition in terms of uncleanness, the language later used for ritual impurity (Leviticus 18:20). The word expresses how deeply the act violated her and her family. It speaks of the wrong done to her, never of any fault in her. Those who care for the wounded today are called to break the kind of silence Jacob kept, to speak up for the one who has been harmed, and to “open thy mouth for the dumb” (Proverbs 31:8).

wordNotes.explanation: The verb tame’ in this stem means to make unclean. It is used of ritual impurity (Leviticus 15:31) and of sexual sin that pollutes persons and land (Leviticus 18:20; Numbers 5:13). The word recurs in verses 13 and 27 and frames the brothers’ grievance. It expresses the violation done to Dinah, the uncleanness attaching to the offender’s act, without implying any guilt on her part.

From charash, to be silent or keep still. It can describe wise restraint (Proverbs 11:12) or culpable silence when speech is needed (Esther 4:14). The verb itself is neutral; the surrounding story shows that Jacob’s stillness left his daughter undefended.

verses.bibleText: And Hamor the father of Shechem went out unto Jacob to commune with him.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Hamor, obeying his son, “went out unto Jacob to commune with him.” The ruler of the city takes the initiative and comes to the encampment as one father to another. On its face this is a diplomatic courtesy, and Hamor will speak politely. Yet he comes with no apology. He arrives to arrange a marriage while the young woman in question remains in his son’s house.

The verse is brief, and the story will not record that Jacob ever answered him. By the time Hamor speaks, Jacob’s sons have arrived and the conversation passes to them (v. 8). The father who should have represented his daughter’s cause leaves it to others. The “going out” of Hamor echoes Dinah’s going out in verse 1, and the scene is set for a negotiation in which everyone speaks except the one most affected. Scripture warns against those who “speak peaceably” while harm lies hidden underneath (Jeremiah 9:8; Psalm 55:21).

wordNotes.term: לְדַבֵּר אִתּוֹ (ledabber itto) — to commune with him
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “to speak with him.” The KJV’s “commune” suggests formal conference, which fits a ruler approaching the head of a clan. The same verb recurs through the chapter as Hamor speaks to the brothers (Genesis 34:8) and to the men of his city (Genesis 34:20). Much is spoken in the chapter; little of it is true.

verses.bibleText: And the sons of Jacob came out of the field when they heard it: and the men were grieved, and they were very wroth, because he had wrought folly in Israel in lying with Jacob's daughter; which thing ought not to be done.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Jacob’s sons come in from the field “when they heard it,” and their reaction is everything their father’s was not. “The men were grieved, and they were very wroth.” The word for “grieved” is rare in this form; Genesis used it of God’s own grief over human wickedness before the flood (6:6). Their anger burns hot. The narrator does not fault them for these feelings. A sister has been violated, and grief and indignation are right responses to such evil.

The verse then gives the narrator’s own judgment, stated through the brothers’ perspective: Shechem “had wrought folly in Israel in lying with Jacob’s daughter; which thing ought not to be done.” “Folly” in Hebrew is far stronger than the English suggests. It is the word Tamar used when she begged Amnon, “do not thou this folly” (2 Samuel 13:12), and the word for the outrage at Gibeah (Judges 20:6, 10). It names a shameless act that tears the moral fabric of a community. “In Israel” is striking, since this is the first time the name given to Jacob at Peniel (32:28) is applied to his household as a people. The crime is set against the standard of the family God has called, a standard that existed before any law was written at Sinai. “Which thing ought not to be done” is a moral verdict: there are acts no custom can make acceptable.

The brothers’ anger is right in its object, yet anger is dangerous even when justified. Paul’s counsel, “Be ye angry, and sin not” (Ephesians 4:26), fits this moment exactly. Their grief is aroused by a real wrong; what they do with that anger will be the test. The chapter will show indignation hardening into hatred and then into slaughter, until Jacob on his deathbed curses not their concern for Dinah but their anger, “for it was fierce,” and their wrath, “for it was cruel” (49:7). There is a righteous anger that refuses to shrug at abuse. It has to be governed by God’s justice, or it becomes a second wrong.

wordNotes.explanation: Nevalah denotes a disgraceful, senseless outrage, especially one that violates sexual or communal norms. It is used of a betrothed woman’s unchastity (Deuteronomy 22:21), Achan’s theft of devoted things (Joshua 7:15), the crime at Gibeah (Judges 20:6), and Amnon’s assault on Tamar (2 Samuel 13:12). The related noun naval describes the “fool” who says there is no God (Psalm 14:1). Folly in this sense is moral and spiritual, a deed that treats God’s order with contempt.

From ‘atsav, to hurt or grieve, here in a reflexive form: they were pained to the heart. The same form describes the Lord’s grief at the corruption of the earth (Genesis 6:6). The brothers feel the wound inflicted on their sister as a personal sorrow, a response the narrator records without reproach.

verses.bibleText: And Hamor communed with them, saying, The soul of my son Shechem longeth for your daughter: I pray you give her him to wife.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Hamor addresses the brothers along with their father, for in that world the father and brothers of a young woman together acted as her guardians, as Laban and Bethuel did for Rebekah (24:50). His opening words are smooth: “The soul of my son Shechem longeth for your daughter: I pray you give her him to wife.” He uses the courteous “I pray you” that his son had omitted (v. 4), and he presents Shechem as a young man in love.

What Hamor leaves out speaks louder than what he says. He offers no word of regret for the crime, makes no mention of the violation, and does not say that Dinah is in his son’s house. He speaks as though a respectable proposal were being made from a respectable beginning. His silence on the wrong implies that he does not regard it as one, or that he expects the family to accept it as the price of good relations with a powerful neighbour. Scripture warns against healing a wound “slightly, saying, Peace, peace; when there is no peace” (Jeremiah 6:14). A settlement that ignores the injury to the victim cannot restore what was broken.

wordNotes.term: חָשְׁקָה נַפְשׁוֹ (chasheqah nafsho) — his soul longeth
wordNotes.explanation: Chashaq means to be attached to, to set one’s desire upon. It is used of a man’s desire for a captive woman (Deuteronomy 21:11) and, remarkably, of the Lord’s setting his love upon Israel by free choice (Deuteronomy 7:7). Hamor uses it to present his son’s craving as devoted love; the context shows a desire that never reckoned with the harm it caused.

verses.bibleText: And make ye marriages with us, and give your daughters unto us, and take our daughters unto you.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Hamor widens the proposal far beyond one marriage: “make ye marriages with us, and give your daughters unto us, and take our daughters unto you.” He offers a full alliance in which the two peoples would intermarry freely. For a Canaanite ruler this was a sensible arrangement. A wealthy clan with large flocks would strengthen his city, and intermarriage would bind them to it.

For the family of Abraham the offer struck at the heart of its calling. Abraham had made his servant swear not to take a wife for Isaac from the Canaanites (24:3), and Isaac had charged Jacob in the same way (28:1). Esau’s Hittite wives had been “a grief of mind” to his parents (26:34-35). The issue was never ethnic pride. God had chosen this family to carry the promise of blessing to all nations (12:3), and absorption into the religion and morals of Canaan would have ended that mission. Later law forbade such marriages for the same reason: “they will turn away thy son from following me” (Deuteronomy 7:3-4).

The door remained open to outsiders who turned to Israel’s God, as Rahab and Ruth later did (Joshua 6:25; Ruth 1:16). What Hamor offers is the opposite movement, Israel dissolved into Canaan. Paul’s principle for believers stands on the same ground: “Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers” (2 Corinthians 6:14).

wordNotes.explanation: From the root chatan, related to the words for son-in-law and father-in-law. In this reflexive stem it means to become related by marriage, to form marriage alliances. It is the verb used when Moses forbids intermarriage with the Canaanites (Deuteronomy 7:3) and when Solomon allies himself with Pharaoh (1 Kings 3:1). The word describes a binding of families and peoples, which is why it carries such weight here.

verses.bibleText: And ye shall dwell with us: and the land shall be before you; dwell and trade ye therein, and get you possessions therein.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Hamor’s offer reaches its most tempting point: “ye shall dwell with us: and the land shall be before you; dwell and trade ye therein, and get you possessions therein.” Jacob had bought one small field (33:19). Now a ruler of the land proposes to open the whole region to him, with rights of residence, free movement for trade, and the right to acquire property.

The phrase “the land shall be before you” recalls Abram’s words to Lot, “Is not the whole land before thee?” (13:9). The verb “get you possessions” belongs to the same family as the word God used when he promised Abraham the land of Canaan “for an everlasting possession” (17:8). Hamor is offering, as a political favour, what God had promised as a gift. The shortcut would have looked like the fulfilment of the covenant, attained without waiting and without conflict. The price, unstated in this speech but plain in verse 23, was the family’s identity.

Abraham had refused even a thread from the king of Sodom so that no one could say a Canaanite had made him rich (14:22-23). Christ faced the same temptation in a greater form when the devil offered him the kingdoms of the world without the cross (Matthew 4:8-10). God’s promises are not to be seized by compromise with the powers that oppose him. The inheritance would come in God’s time, and for Abraham’s true seed it reaches beyond Canaan to the earth made new (Romans 4:13; Hebrews 11:9-10).

wordNotes.explanation: From ’achaz, to grasp or take hold, here in a stem meaning to acquire property, to be settled as owners. The noun ’achuzzah, “possession,” is the word of God’s land promise (Genesis 17:8) and of Abraham’s purchased burial ground (Genesis 23:20). Hamor dangles a human route to what God had pledged; Israel would later be “possessed” of the land only through God’s gift (Leviticus 25:24).

The verb sachar means to go about, to travel around, and so to trade as a merchant. It is related to the word for merchants who traverse the land (Genesis 23:16; Genesis 37:28). Hamor promises freedom of movement and commerce throughout his territory, an attractive economic benefit for a pastoral clan.

verses.bibleText: And Shechem said unto her father and unto her brethren, Let me find grace in your eyes, and what ye shall say unto me I will give.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Now Shechem speaks for himself, addressing “her father” and “her brethren.” His tone has changed from the curt demand of verse 4. “Let me find grace in your eyes, and what ye shall say unto me I will give.” It is the language of a suppliant seeking favour, the same expression Jacob had used when he approached Esau with his gifts (32:5; 33:8, 10).

The resemblance is instructive. Jacob had wronged Esau and came seeking reconciliation, and Esau received him with grace. Shechem has wronged Dinah and her family and comes seeking favour. But the two approaches differ in a decisive way. Jacob bowed seven times and called himself Esau’s servant, acknowledging his fault in action if not in words. Shechem makes no confession and offers to pay whatever price is named. Favour is sought as a transaction. Scripture holds that covering a sin and confessing it lead to opposite outcomes (Proverbs 28:13). An open hand with money cannot take the place of an honest admission of wrong.

wordNotes.explanation: To “find grace (chen) in the eyes” of someone is a common Hebrew idiom for gaining a superior’s favour or goodwill. Noah found grace in the eyes of the Lord (Genesis 6:8), and Jacob used the phrase repeatedly before Esau (Genesis 33:8). Here it is a polite formula of request, spoken by one seeking a favour he has done nothing to deserve.

verses.bibleText: Ask me never so much dowry and gift, and I will give according as ye shall say unto me: but give me the damsel to wife.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Shechem presses his offer to the limit: “Ask me never so much dowry and gift, and I will give according as ye shall say unto me: but give me the damsel to wife.” The “dowry” was the bride-price a bridegroom paid to the young woman’s family, a recognised part of marriage in the ancient world. Jacob himself had paid for Rachel and Leah with fourteen years of labour (29:18-27). The “gift” was an additional present to the bride or her family, like the jewels and garments Abraham’s servant gave Rebekah and her household (24:53).

Shechem’s generosity has some standing in law. Moses would later require a man who violated an unbetrothed young woman to pay her father a substantial sum, marry her, and never divorce her (Exodus 22:16-17; Deuteronomy 22:28-29). In a culture where an unmarried woman who had been violated faced lasting disgrace and poverty, such provisions aimed at her protection. To that extent Shechem is offering what custom expected of him.

Yet the offer is made under pressure, while Dinah remains in his house (v. 26), and it comes without acknowledgment of guilt. The brothers will later say that he dealt with their sister “as with an harlot” (v. 31), a charge that reads his open-ended payment as an attempt to buy what he had already taken. Money can compensate for some losses, but it cannot purchase a person or erase a violation. Christ’s redemption stands in sharp contrast: he paid the price for his bride with his own blood, giving himself for her (Ephesians 5:25; 1 Peter 1:18-19).

wordNotes.term: מֹהַר וּמַתָּן (mohar umattan) — dowry and gift
wordNotes.explanation: Mohar is the bride-price paid by the groom to the bride’s family, mentioned also in Exodus 22:17 and in Saul’s demand of David (1 Samuel 18:25). Mattan is a gift or present (Proverbs 18:16). Together they describe a generous marriage settlement. Shechem’s open offer, “ask me never so much,” shows how far he was willing to go, while leaving the wrong itself unaddressed.

verses.bibleText: And the sons of Jacob answered Shechem and Hamor his father deceitfully, and said, because he had defiled Dinah their sister:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Before reporting the brothers’ answer, the narrator tells the reader how to hear it: “the sons of Jacob answered Shechem and Hamor his father deceitfully.” Every word they say in verses 14-17 is to be weighed against this warning. The explanation follows at once, “because he had defiled Dinah their sister.” Their motive is the wrong done to her; their method is a lie.

The word “deceitfully” carries a family history. Isaac used it when he told Esau, “Thy brother came with subtilty, and hath taken away thy blessing” (27:35). Jacob had deceived his father; Laban had deceived Jacob (29:25); now Jacob’s sons deceive their neighbours. The pattern of the household is repeating itself in the next generation. Sins that are never fully dealt with in a family have a way of resurfacing in the children (Exodus 20:5), though each person remains responsible for his own choices (Ezekiel 18:20).

It is notable that Jacob does not answer. Hamor had come to speak with him (v. 6), and Shechem had addressed “her father and … her brethren” (v. 11), yet the reply comes from the sons alone. Jacob’s later protest (v. 30) and his deathbed words, “O my soul, come not thou into their secret” (49:6), suggest that he had no part in the plot. His silence, though, left the field to them.

The brothers had a real grievance and a legitimate concern. Their sister was held in the house of the man who had violated her, and they were bargaining with a powerful ruler. Deceit in such a setting may look like the only weapon of the weak. Scripture gives no such licence. The God of Israel is “a God of truth” (Deuteronomy 32:4), and his people are to speak truth even to their enemies (Psalm 15:2-4; Ephesians 4:25). Justice pursued by treachery becomes another injustice.

wordNotes.explanation: Mirmah means deceit, treachery, fraud. It is always a negative word in Scripture: false balances are “deceitful” (Proverbs 11:1), and the Servant of the Lord had no “deceit in his mouth” (Isaiah 53:9). In Genesis it first describes Jacob’s theft of the blessing (Genesis 27:35); its return here marks the sons as heirs of their father’s old way. Jesus called Nathanael “an Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile,” the opposite of this inheritance (John 1:47).

verses.bibleText: And they said unto them, We cannot do this thing, to give our sister to one that is uncircumcised; for that were a reproach unto us:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The brothers’ stated objection sounds principled: “We cannot do this thing, to give our sister to one that is uncircumcised; for that were a reproach unto us.” On its own terms the statement is true. Circumcision was the sign God gave Abraham, marking every male of his household as belonging to the covenant (17:10-14). An uncircumcised man stood outside that covenant, and marriage to him would have meant the family’s daughter passing outside the people of promise.

What the brothers do not say is equally revealing. They do not mention the assault. They do not demand Dinah’s release. They do not say that Shechem’s act has disqualified him. They reduce the whole matter to a question of ritual status, as if the only obstacle to the marriage were a missing mark on the body. This framing conceals their real aim and, at the same time, treats the covenant sign as a tribal badge that anyone could acquire. A sign meant to express belonging to the God of Abraham becomes a bargaining point.

“Reproach” is the word for disgrace or shame. Later Israel would use “uncircumcised” as a term of contempt for its enemies (1 Samuel 17:26), and Joshua would speak of rolling away “the reproach of Egypt” when the nation was circumcised at Gilgal (Joshua 5:9). The brothers invoke a genuine conviction, but they use it as a cover. Truth spoken in order to deceive is still a form of lying. Words that are accurate in themselves can serve a false purpose, and God looks at the heart that speaks them (1 Samuel 16:7; Proverbs 26:24-26).

wordNotes.explanation: ‘Orlah means foreskin; “one that hath a foreskin” is the literal sense of the phrase rendered “uncircumcised.” The word appears in the institution of circumcision (Genesis 17:11, 14) and is later applied figuratively to hearts, ears, and lips that will not respond to God (Deuteronomy 10:16; Jeremiah 6:10). That figurative use reveals what the sign was meant to signify all along: a heart surrendered to God.

Cherpah means disgrace, scorn, or shame. Rachel used it when God removed her barrenness, “God hath taken away my reproach” (Genesis 30:23), and Joshua when Israel’s circumcision was renewed (Joshua 5:9). The brothers present marriage to an uncircumcised man as a public shame upon the family.

verses.bibleText: But in this will we consent unto you: If ye will be as we be, that every male of you be circumcised;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The brothers now state their condition: “If ye will be as we be, that every male of you be circumcised.” Not only Shechem but every male of the city must undergo the rite. On the surface the demand seems to offer the Shechemites full membership in the family of Abraham. Underneath, it is a trap. Grown men recovering from circumcision would be unable to fight for several days, and the brothers knew it.

Here lies the gravest aspect of their sin. Circumcision was “a token of the covenant” between God and Abraham’s descendants (17:11), a sign of the Lord’s promise and of the household’s dedication to him. It was never a mere physical procedure or a mark of ethnicity. Abraham had circumcised Ishmael and the servants of his house because they were joined to his worship of the Lord (17:23-27). Later, a foreigner who wished to share the Passover was to be circumcised as a step of genuine allegiance to Israel’s God (Exodus 12:48). The brothers ask for the sign without the faith it signified, and they do so as the means of a massacre. They turn a sacred ordinance into a weapon.

The prophets and apostles would insist that the outward sign without inward reality counts for nothing. Moses urged Israel to circumcise the foreskin of their heart (Deuteronomy 10:16), Jeremiah warned that the circumcised could be uncircumcised in heart (Jeremiah 9:25-26), and Paul declared that true circumcision “is that of the heart, in the spirit” (Romans 2:28-29). The episode at Shechem is a stark early example of how religious forms can be emptied of meaning and even made to serve violence. Christians have their own sacred signs, and the warning applies to them as well: baptism and the Lord’s Supper belong to those who come in faith, never to manipulation or coercion.

wordNotes.explanation: From mul, to cut around, in the passive stem: to be circumcised. It is the verb of Genesis 17:10-13, where God commands every male of Abraham’s household to be circumcised as the covenant sign. Its use here in a deceitful bargain stands in pointed contrast with that solemn institution. Later, Moses and Paul apply the verb to the heart (Deuteronomy 30:6; Romans 2:29).

From ’ut, to agree or consent, a verb found only in this chapter (Genesis 34:15, 22-23) and in 2 Kings 12:8. It describes an agreement reached by negotiation. Its repetition highlights that the whole narrative is about terms and bargains rather than truth.

verses.bibleText: Then will we give our daughters unto you, and we will take your daughters to us, and we will dwell with you, and we will become one people.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The brothers echo Hamor’s own terms back to him: “Then will we give our daughters unto you, and we will take your daughters to us, and we will dwell with you, and we will become one people.” They promise exactly what Hamor proposed in verses 9-10 and add the climactic phrase, “one people.” The offer sounds complete and generous.

It was also a lie, and a dangerous one even if it had been sincere. To become “one people” with Shechem would have meant the end of the distinct family through whom God had promised to bless the nations. The language recalls Babel, where humanity said “the people is one” and sought a unity apart from God (11:6). The brothers say the words they know Hamor wants to hear while planning something else entirely. Scripture describes such a tongue as “a sharp sword” hidden under smooth speech (Psalm 57:4; 55:21). The irony is heavy: the very unity they pretend to offer is what the covenant forbade, and the treachery they intend is what God hates.

wordNotes.explanation: ‘Am echad means a single people or nation. The same phrase describes united humanity at Babel (Genesis 11:6). God intended Abraham’s family to become a great people set apart (Genesis 12:2), and through it to bless all nations; merging with Shechem would have undone that calling. The phrase recurs in Hamor’s speech to his city (Genesis 34:22).

verses.bibleText: But if ye will not hearken unto us, to be circumcised; then will we take our daughter, and we will be gone.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The brothers close with an alternative: “But if ye will not hearken unto us, to be circumcised; then will we take our daughter, and we will be gone.” The phrase “our daughter” is unusual on the lips of brothers. They speak as the family’s representatives, taking the place their father has left empty.

The threat is hollow in one sense, for Dinah is in Shechem’s house and the brothers have no immediate means of removing her. Yet it puts pressure on Shechem, who wants her badly, and makes refusal seem costly. The trap is set with care: the Shechemites are offered a gain they want and a loss they fear, and the deceit is complete. Proverbs warns that the one who digs a pit for others often falls into it himself (Proverbs 26:27), and the chapter will show how much this scheme costs Jacob’s own household in its standing among the nations of the land.

wordNotes.explanation: Bat with the suffix “our”: our daughter. Since Jacob is the father, the brothers’ use of “our daughter” shows them speaking for the whole household, assuming the authority their father has not exercised. In verse 31 they will call her “our sister” (Genesis 34:31), again stressing their own bond with her in contrast to Jacob’s silence (Genesis 34:5).

verses.bibleText: And their words pleased Hamor, and Shechem Hamor's son.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Their words pleased Hamor, and Shechem Hamor’s son.” The proposal seemed reasonable to both. Hamor saw political and economic advantage; Shechem saw the way to obtain Dinah. Neither seems to have suspected deceit, and neither showed any interest in the God whose covenant sign they were about to accept.

The pleasure of the moment blinded them. Satisfaction with an agreement does not make it sound, and the ease with which they consented shows how lightly they regarded the meaning of what was asked. To them circumcision was a small inconvenience, a few days of pain in exchange for a bride, a wealthy ally, and herds that might one day be theirs (v. 23). They measured the proposal entirely by what it would bring them. Men who treat sacred things as tools of advantage are easily deceived by others who do the same, and here both parties were playing that game. “There is a way that seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death” (Proverbs 14:12).

wordNotes.term: וַיִּיטְבוּ דִבְרֵיהֶם (wayyitevu divrehem) — and their words pleased
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “their words were good in the eyes of.” The idiom expresses approval, used when Joseph’s counsel pleased Pharaoh (Genesis 41:37) and when a plan seemed right to a ruler (1 Samuel 18:20). What seems good in human eyes may be a snare, as the next verses will show.

verses.bibleText: And the young man deferred not to do the thing, because he had delight in Jacob's daughter: and he was more honourable than all the house of his father.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Shechem acts at once: “the young man deferred not to do the thing, because he had delight in Jacob’s daughter.” His haste in being circumcised mirrors his haste in seizing Dinah. Desire drives him in both cases. He undergoes the covenant sign without any recorded thought of the God it represented, solely because he wants the young woman.

The narrator adds, “and he was more honourable than all the house of his father.” The word means weighty, respected, of high standing. Shechem was the most influential member of his family, the heir apparent, and his readiness to be circumcised would carry weight with the rest of the city. That is the point of the remark: his prominence explains why the townsmen follow his example. It is a statement about his rank, not a verdict on his moral character, which the chapter has already exposed.

There is a sad irony here. A man of honour in the eyes of his city had acted shamefully toward a defenceless young woman. Human standing and moral worth are different things, and God “seeth not as man seeth” (1 Samuel 16:7). The word “honourable” also stands in contrast to the “folly” of verse 7: the most honoured man in Shechem had committed the most dishonourable act. Christ reversed the world’s order when he taught that true greatness is found in serving others (Mark 10:42-45).

wordNotes.explanation: From kavad, to be heavy, in the sense of weighty or honoured. The passive participle describes a person of standing and influence, as with Jabez, who “was more honourable than his brethren” (1 Chronicles 4:9). Here it marks Shechem’s social rank, which gave his example force with the men of the city (Genesis 34:20).

Chafets means to take pleasure in or desire. It is used of the Lord’s delight in mercy (Micah 7:18) and of a husband’s delight in a wife (Deuteronomy 21:14). Here it names Shechem’s intense desire for Dinah, the motive that drives his swift circumcision.

verses.bibleText: And Hamor and Shechem his son came unto the gate of their city, and communed with the men of their city, saying,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Hamor and Shechem take the proposal to “the gate of their city,” where they “communed with the men of their city.” The city gate was the place of public business in the ancient world. Elders sat there to judge cases and witness transactions; Abraham bought the cave of Machpelah “in the audience of … all that went in at the gate of his city” (23:10, 18), and Boaz settled Ruth’s redemption before the elders at the gate (Ruth 4:1-11).

A decision affecting every male in the city required public consent, and the two leaders now become advocates. Their task is delicate. They must persuade grown men to undergo a painful rite for the sake of an alliance, and they must do it without admitting that the real reason is the prince’s desire for a woman he has wronged. What follows in verses 21-23 is a carefully shaped speech that tells the townsmen what they want to hear. Those who had just been deceived now become deceivers themselves.

wordNotes.explanation: The city gate was the civic centre of ancient towns, where legal cases were heard, contracts witnessed, and public decisions made (Genesis 23:10; Deuteronomy 21:19). Lot sat in the gate of Sodom as a man of standing (Genesis 19:1). The prophets called for justice to be established “in the gate” (Amos 5:15), making it the place where a community’s righteousness or corruption became visible.

verses.bibleText: These men are peaceable with us; therefore let them dwell in the land, and trade therein; for the land, behold, it is large enough for them; let us take their daughters to us for wives, and let us give them our daughters.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Hamor’s speech to the townsmen begins with reassurance: “These men are peaceable with us.” The word “peaceable” is related to shalom and to the word used when Jacob came “in peace” or “safely” to Shechem (33:18). Hamor believes what he says, and the narrator’s irony is sharp. The family he describes as peaceful is at that moment planning the city’s destruction. He has been thoroughly deceived, as deceivers often are.

He continues: “therefore let them dwell in the land, and trade therein; for the land, behold, it is large enough for them.” He presents the newcomers as no threat to the townsmen’s livelihood. There is room enough for everyone. The phrase echoes the problem of chapter 13, where the land could not bear Abram and Lot together (13:6), but here it is the Canaanites who generously make space.

Then comes the marriage proposal, now phrased from the city’s side: “let us take their daughters to us for wives, and let us give them our daughters.” Hamor has reversed the order of his speech to Jacob, where he began with Jacob giving daughters (v. 9). Speaking to his own people, he puts their gain first. A subtle omission is also worth noting. In verse 10 he had offered Jacob’s family the right to “get you possessions” in the land. Before the townsmen he says nothing about property rights for the newcomers. Each audience hears the version best suited to win its consent. Smooth talk that tailors the truth to each listener is a mark of the double-tongued, whom Scripture warns against (1 Timothy 3:8; James 3:10).

wordNotes.explanation: Shalem means whole, complete, at peace. It describes a heart wholly devoted to God (1 Kings 8:61) and relations free of hostility. The related form appears in Genesis 33:18, where Jacob arrived “safe” or “in peace” at Shechem. Hamor’s confidence that Jacob’s family is shalem toward his city turns bitterly ironic in verse 25, and Psalm 55:20 speaks of one who “hath put forth his hands against such as be at peace with him.”

verses.bibleText: Only herein will the men consent unto us for to dwell with us, to be one people, if every male among us be circumcised, as they are circumcised.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Hamor now mentions the condition, and he presents it as a small matter: “Only herein will the men consent unto us for to dwell with us, to be one people, if every male among us be circumcised, as they are circumcised.” The word “only” minimises the demand. Circumcision is placed in the middle of the speech, framed by the benefits on either side, as though it were a trifling formality.

To the men of Shechem it was exactly that. They had no thought of turning to the God of Abraham or of accepting the obligations of his covenant. The sign was to them an entrance fee to an advantageous union. Both sides in the negotiation, then, treated circumcision as something other than what God intended: the brothers used it as a trap, and the Shechemites accepted it as a business term. The sign that marked Abraham’s faith (Romans 4:11) had been severed from faith altogether. Paul would warn the churches of Galatia against those who pressed circumcision on others for appearance’s sake, “that they may glory in your flesh” (Galatians 6:12-13). Outward religion without inward allegiance is always vulnerable to this kind of misuse.

wordNotes.term: הִמּוֹל לָנוּ כָּל־זָכָר (himmol lanu kol-zakhar) — every male among us be circumcised
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase deliberately echoes the original command to Abraham, “every man child among you shall be circumcised” (Genesis 17:10). The repetition of “every male” in verses 15, 22, 24, and 25 draws attention to the totality of the rite and to the totality of the massacre that follows. The words of the covenant are now spoken in a Canaanite assembly, for wholly different ends.

verses.bibleText: Shall not their cattle and their substance and every beast of their's be our's? only let us consent unto them, and they will dwell with us.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Hamor saves his strongest argument for the end: “Shall not their cattle and their substance and every beast of their’s be our’s?” Here at last is the motive he did not mention to Jacob’s family. The alliance would, in time, absorb Jacob’s wealth into the city. Through intermarriage and settlement, the flocks and herds that God had multiplied for Jacob in Paddan-aram (30:43) would become Shechemite property.

The contrast with Hamor’s speech to the brothers is stark. To them he offered land, trade, and possessions (v. 10); to his own people he promises the newcomers’ possessions. The same deal is sold to each side as a gain at the other’s expense. Hamor, the ruler who had come to make amends for his son’s act, is revealed as a calculating politician. The townsmen, for their part, are moved by greed. They agree to the rite not out of friendship or respect but because they expect to profit.

“Only let us consent unto them, and they will dwell with us.” The closing appeal sounds generous, but its foundation is covetousness. The tenth commandment forbids coveting a neighbour’s “ox” and “ass” and “any thing that is thy neighbour’s” (Exodus 20:17), and the men of Shechem are planning to do exactly that. Jesus warned, “Take heed, and beware of covetousness” (Luke 12:15), for greed blinds people to danger. The city that agreed to be circumcised in order to seize Jacob’s cattle would lose its own cattle, and much more besides (vv. 28-29).

wordNotes.term: מִקְנֵהֶם וְקִנְיָנָם (miqnehem weqinyanam) — their cattle and their substance
wordNotes.explanation: Miqneh is livestock, the wealth of a pastoral family (Genesis 13:2); qinyan is acquired property or goods, from the verb qanah, to acquire. Jacob had brought both from Paddan-aram (Genesis 31:18). The pairing summarises everything Jacob owned, which the Shechemites hoped to absorb.

verses.bibleText: And unto Hamor and unto Shechem his son hearkened all that went out of the gate of his city; and every male was circumcised, all that went out of the gate of his city.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The persuasion succeeds: “unto Hamor and unto Shechem his son hearkened all that went out of the gate of his city; and every male was circumcised, all that went out of the gate of his city.” The repeated phrase “all that went out of the gate of his city” probably refers to the able-bodied men, those who went out to work the fields and to defend the town. The repetition underlines that every one of them submitted.

It is a remarkable demonstration of how readily a community follows its leaders. Hamor and Shechem held authority and prestige (v. 19), and the men trusted them. Throughout Scripture the people tend to go where their rulers lead, for good or ill. Jeroboam’s golden calves drew Israel into idolatry (1 Kings 12:28-30); Josiah’s reform brought the nation back to the covenant (2 Kings 23:1-3). Leaders carry a heavy responsibility, and followers must test what they are told rather than simply going along.

The men of the city now bore the sign of a covenant they did not understand and had no intention of keeping. The rite left them temporarily helpless. By accepting a sacred sign for the sake of gain, they had unknowingly made themselves defenceless before those who meant them harm.

wordNotes.term: כָּל־יֹצְאֵי שַׁעַר עִירוֹ (kol-yots’e sha‘ar ‘iro) — all that went out of the gate of his city
wordNotes.explanation: A Hebrew expression closely related to “all that went in at the gate of his city” (Genesis 23:10, 18), which describes the full citizens of a town. Here “going out” may emphasise the working and fighting men who went out from the city. The phrase is repeated within the verse to stress that no able-bodied man was left uncircumcised, setting the stage for verse 25.

verses.bibleText: And it came to pass on the third day, when they were sore, that two of the sons of Jacob, Simeon and Levi, Dinah's brethren, took each man his sword, and came upon the city boldly, and slew all the males.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And it came to pass on the third day, when they were sore.” The timing is deliberate. Adult circumcision would leave men in pain and feverish for some days, and the third day was likely the worst. When Israel was circumcised at Gilgal, the people stayed in camp “till they were whole” (Joshua 5:8). Simeon and Levi chose the moment of greatest weakness.

The two attackers are named with precision: “Simeon and Levi, Dinah’s brethren.” They were her full brothers, sons of Leah, and their kinship explains their fury. They “took each man his sword, and came upon the city boldly, and slew all the males.” The word “boldly” can also mean “securely” or “unawares”; the city felt safe and was caught off guard. The two may have had servants with them, but the narrator focuses on these two men and their swords. The verb “took” returns, the same verb used of Shechem taking Dinah (v. 2). The brothers now take swords, and the taking multiplies.

This is the moral centre of the chapter, and the verdict of Scripture on it is unmistakable. When Jacob blessed his sons before his death, he did not bless these two; he spoke of their weapons as “instruments of cruelty,” said “in their anger they slew a man,” and declared, “Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce; and their wrath, for it was cruel” (49:5-7). The punishment of one guilty man became the slaughter of an entire male population, most of whom had done nothing to Dinah. The massacre had no divine command behind it. It was personal vengeance, carried out under cover of a sacred rite, against people who had trusted the brothers’ word.

The Lord had told Abraham that the iniquity of the Amorites was not yet full and that judgment on Canaan would come in God’s time (15:16). Simeon and Levi seized that judgment for themselves, generations early and for their own cause. Scripture repeatedly reserves vengeance for God: “To me belongeth vengeance” (Deuteronomy 32:35), and Paul applies it directly, “avenge not yourselves” (Romans 12:19).

Yet grace would have the final word in Levi’s story. His descendants, scattered in Israel as Jacob foretold, were scattered as priests among the tribes after they stood with the Lord at Sinai (Exodus 32:26-29; Joshua 21:3). Zeal turned to God’s service replaced zeal turned to murder. Christ, the true Priest, would take the violence of the world upon himself rather than inflict it, and pray for those who struck him (Luke 23:34).

wordNotes.term: בִּהְיוֹתָם כֹּאֲבִים (bihyotam ko’avim) — when they were sore
wordNotes.explanation: Ko’evim is the participle of ka’av, to be in pain. It describes physical suffering (Job 14:22) and inward anguish (Psalm 69:29). The phrase pinpoints the men’s condition after circumcision: weakened and in pain, unable to defend themselves. Joshua 5:8 describes Israel resting in camp after its own mass circumcision until the men recovered.

Betach means security or confidence. It can describe the attackers’ boldness or, more likely here, the city’s sense of safety: they came upon a city that was “secure,” unsuspecting. The word describes Laish, attacked while it dwelt “careless … quiet and secure” (Judges 18:7, 27), and Israel dwelling “in safety” under God’s care (Deuteronomy 33:28).

verses.bibleText: And they slew Hamor and Shechem his son with the edge of the sword, and took Dinah out of Shechem's house, and went out.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The narrator singles out two victims by name: “they slew Hamor and Shechem his son with the edge of the sword.” The ruler who had negotiated and the prince who had committed the crime die with the rest. Then comes a detail that changes how the whole negotiation must be read: they “took Dinah out of Shechem’s house, and went out.” Throughout the bargaining, Dinah had been in Shechem’s house. Hamor’s courtesy, Shechem’s generous offers, and the city’s debate all took place while the young woman at the centre of them was held by the man who had violated her.

This disclosure explains much of the brothers’ fury and lends weight to their later question in verse 31. Shechem’s proposal was made from a position of strength, with Dinah in his power. Whatever affection he felt, he had not released her to her family before seeking her hand. Her rescue was right. The family had every reason to want her home, and the law later given to Israel would treat the forcible holding of a woman as a grave wrong (Deuteronomy 22:25-27).

Yet the rescue came at the cost of a massacre, and that cost is the narrator’s concern. The verbs echo the opening of the chapter in reverse. Dinah “went out” and was “taken” (vv. 1-2); now Simeon and Levi “took” her and “went out.” The reversal is complete, and it has been achieved by blood. A just end does not sanctify unjust means. Scripture never accepts that evil may be done that good may come (Romans 3:8).

Dinah herself remains silent even now. She is carried home without a recorded word, and after this chapter she appears only in the list of those who went down to Egypt (46:15). Her story is left unfinished in Scripture, a reminder that the wounds of violence often outlast the events that caused them. The God who “healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds” (Psalm 147:3) is able to carry what the text leaves untold.

wordNotes.term: לְפִי־חָרֶב (lefi-charev) — with the edge of the sword
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “according to the mouth of the sword,” a Hebrew idiom picturing the sword as devouring its victims. It recurs in descriptions of total destruction in war (Joshua 6:21; Judges 1:8; 1 Samuel 15:8). Its use here marks the killing as a full military assault, carried out without divine commission.

verses.bibleText: The sons of Jacob came upon the slain, and spoiled the city, because they had defiled their sister.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“The sons of Jacob came upon the slain, and spoiled the city, because they had defiled their sister.” The circle widens. Simeon and Levi carried out the killing; now “the sons of Jacob,” apparently the other brothers as well, descend on the dead and plunder the town. What began as two brothers’ vengeance becomes the whole family’s profit.

The reason given, “because they had defiled their sister,” is significant. The verb is now plural. Shechem alone had violated Dinah (v. 2), but the brothers hold the entire city responsible. Perhaps they reasoned that the townsmen had shared in the crime by accepting it without protest and seeking to profit from it. Yet the text has given no hint that the men of the city had any part in what Shechem did, and holding a whole population accountable for one man’s act is precisely the kind of collective vengeance that Scripture condemns. Later law insisted that “the fathers shall not be put to death for the children, neither shall the children be put to death for the fathers: every man shall be put to death for his own sin” (Deuteronomy 24:16).

There is also a bitter irony. The brothers were outraged that Dinah had been defiled, yet they now defile themselves by stripping the bodies of the dead, an act that would later render a person unclean (Numbers 19:11-16). Their concern for purity has become selective. Jesus exposed the same contradiction in the religious leaders of his day, who strained at a gnat and swallowed a camel (Matthew 23:24). Zeal for one point of righteousness can blind a person to gross unrighteousness in himself.

wordNotes.explanation: From bazaz, to plunder or take as booty. It describes the looting that follows conquest (Numbers 31:9; Deuteronomy 2:35). Abraham had refused plunder after his victory over the kings (Genesis 14:22-23), and the contrast with his descendants here is stark. In Esther the Jews pointedly “laid not their hands on the prey” after defending themselves (Esther 9:10).

verses.bibleText: They took their sheep, and their oxen, and their asses, and that which was in the city, and that which was in the field,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The inventory of plunder begins: “They took their sheep, and their oxen, and their asses, and that which was in the city, and that which was in the field.” The list is deliberately thorough, moving from flocks and herds to the city and the countryside. Nothing is left.

The list also completes the irony of Hamor’s speech. He had asked the townsmen, “Shall not their cattle and their substance and every beast of their’s be our’s?” (v. 23). Now the opposite has happened: the Shechemites’ cattle and beasts belong to Jacob’s sons. The plan to absorb Jacob’s wealth has ended with Shechem’s wealth absorbed into Jacob’s camp. Covetousness has met its reward (Proverbs 1:19). Yet the brothers are no better than those they plundered. They too have taken what was not theirs, and the repeated verb “took” now covers sheep, oxen, asses, and goods. The family that God had promised to make a blessing to the nations (12:3) has become a curse to its neighbours.

wordNotes.explanation: Laqach, to take, is one of the chapter’s key verbs. Shechem “took” Dinah (Genesis 34:2), asked his father to “get” (take) her (Genesis 34:4), the brothers threatened to “take” her and go (Genesis 34:17), and Simeon and Levi “took” their swords (Genesis 34:25). Now the brothers take everything. The repeated verb traces the spread of grasping from one man’s act to a whole family’s.

verses.bibleText: And all their wealth, and all their little ones, and their wives took they captive, and spoiled even all that was in the house.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The plunder extends to people: “And all their wealth, and all their little ones, and their wives took they captive, and spoiled even all that was in the house.” The women and children of Shechem are carried off as captives. The outrage that began with one young woman taken by force ends with many women and children taken by force.

This is the darkest symmetry in the chapter. The brothers had protested that their sister was treated as an object to be bought (v. 31); they now treat the women of Shechem as possessions to be seized. Shechem had wanted Jacob’s daughters given to the Shechemites (v. 9); instead the Shechemites’ wives and children are taken by Jacob’s sons. The sin they hated in Shechem they reproduce on a larger scale. Evil answered by evil multiplies.

The chapter offers no word of comfort for these captives, and the silence is its own judgment. Widows and orphans were made in a single day for the wrong of one man. God would later command his people to defend the fatherless and the widow (Exodus 22:22-24; Isaiah 1:17), and Christ’s concern for the helpless reveals the heart of the God whom Jacob’s sons had dishonoured. Paul’s instruction, “Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good” (Romans 12:21), names the path the brothers refused.

wordNotes.explanation: Taf refers to young children, those who walk with short steps. It appears in descriptions of families on the move (Genesis 43:8; Genesis 50:21) and of the vulnerable spared or taken in war (Numbers 31:9). Jacob had spoken of his own children as “tender” and needing gentle care on the journey (Genesis 33:13); here other families’ little ones are carried off as plunder.

From shavah, to take captive. The verb describes the capture of Lot by the eastern kings (Genesis 14:14) and the carrying off of David’s family at Ziklag (1 Samuel 30:2). It marks the brothers’ act as an act of war against the defenceless.

verses.bibleText: And Jacob said to Simeon and Levi, Ye have troubled me to make me to stink among the inhabitants of the land, among the Canaanites and the Perizzites: and I being few in number, they shall gather themselves together against me, and slay me; and I shall be destroyed, I and my house.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Jacob finally speaks, and his first recorded words in the whole affair are addressed to Simeon and Levi: “Ye have troubled me to make me to stink among the inhabitants of the land, among the Canaanites and the Perizzites: and I being few in number, they shall gather themselves together against me, and slay me; and I shall be destroyed, I and my house.”

The rebuke is real, and its fears were well founded. A small clan that had massacred a city could expect the surrounding peoples to unite against it. Jacob’s phrase “make me to stink” is a vivid idiom for becoming odious, hated, a byword among neighbours (Exodus 5:21; 1 Samuel 13:4). “Troubled” is the word used of Achan, who brought disaster on Israel by his sin and gave his name to the valley of Achor, “trouble” (Joshua 7:25-26).

Yet the speech is also revealing for what it lacks. Jacob says nothing about Dinah. He offers no word about the crime against her, the deceit in the use of circumcision, the slaughter of innocent men, or the women and children taken captive. Every concern is for himself: “me,” “I,” “my house.” The first person runs through the verse again and again. His objection is practical and prudential, centred on danger and reputation. Even in rebuking his sons, Jacob does not name their sin as sin against God.

A fuller judgment would come later. On his deathbed Jacob would say of Simeon and Levi, “O my soul, come not thou into their secret … for in their anger they slew a man” (49:5-7). By then he could see their deed for what it was. Here, in the immediate aftermath, he sees mainly the threat. Fear has replaced the faith that had wrestled with God at Peniel.

God’s grace is the surprise that follows. In the next chapter the Lord calls Jacob to Bethel, Jacob puts away the foreign gods in his household, and as they travel “the terror of God was upon the cities that were round about them, and they did not pursue after the sons of Jacob” (35:5). The danger Jacob feared was real, but God protected a family that did not deserve protection. The covenant promise stood because it rested on God’s faithfulness, not on the faithfulness of Jacob or his sons (2 Timothy 2:13).

wordNotes.explanation: ‘Akhar means to stir up trouble, to bring disaster upon. It is used of Achan, whose sin “troubled” Israel (Joshua 7:25), giving its name to the valley of Achor, and of Ahab as “he that troubleth Israel” (1 Kings 18:17-18). Hosea promises that the valley of Achor will become “a door of hope” (Hosea 2:15), a hint that God can redeem even the trouble his people bring on themselves.

wordNotes.term: לְהַבְאִישֵׁנִי (lehav’isheni) — to make me to stink
wordNotes.explanation: From ba’ash, to stink, in a causative stem: to make odious. It is used of Israel becoming abhorrent to Pharaoh (Exodus 5:21), of Saul’s Israel becoming odious to the Philistines (1 Samuel 13:4), and of David becoming hateful to Ammon (2 Samuel 10:6). Jacob fears that the massacre has made his name repugnant throughout the land.

verses.bibleText: And they said, Should he deal with our sister as with an harlot?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The brothers have the last word: “Should he deal with our sister as with an harlot?” The chapter ends on a question, and it is left unanswered. Jacob does not reply.

The question deserves to be heard. In the brothers’ eyes Shechem had treated Dinah as a prostitute, a woman to be used and then paid for. His forceful taking of her, his detention of her in his house, and his offer to pay any price for her all fit that description. The brothers grasped what their father seemed unable to say: a terrible wrong had been done to their sister, and it could not be treated as a business matter. The question is a protest against indifference to sexual violence, and in that respect it is right. The answer to it is “No.” No woman should be dealt with in that way.

The narrator gives the brothers the last word, but not the final verdict. A rhetorical question is not a justification for deceit and mass killing. The question rightly condemns Shechem, but it does not answer Jacob’s complaint or excuse the slaughter of a city, the misuse of the covenant sign, or the captivity of women and children. Scripture supplies the verdict elsewhere. Jacob’s dying words curse the brothers’ anger and wrath (49:5-7), and the tribe of Simeon later became small and was absorbed within Judah (Joshua 19:1). The two most zealous defenders of their sister’s honour lost the leadership that might have been theirs.

The chapter thus closes with two inadequate responses to evil set side by side. Jacob stayed silent when he should have spoken and spoke chiefly of himself when he finally did. His sons spoke with fury and acted with treachery and bloodshed. One offered passivity, the other vengeance, and neither offered justice tempered by truth and mercy. Neither honoured God. It is significant that God’s name does not appear anywhere in this chapter. The family that bore his covenant sign acted as though he were absent.

The gospel answers the brothers’ question in a way they could not. God takes the violation of the vulnerable with utmost seriousness; he will judge every wrong (Ecclesiastes 12:14; Revelation 20:12). Yet he also forbids his people to take vengeance into their own hands, because judgment belongs to him (Romans 12:19). In Christ he bore the full weight of human violence and offered forgiveness even to those who wronged him. Those who have suffered as Dinah did can find in him a Saviour who knows what it is to be shamed and stripped (Hebrews 12:2), and who promises a day when he will wipe away every tear (Revelation 21:4).

wordNotes.explanation: Zonah is a prostitute, a woman who sells sexual favours, from zanah, to commit fornication or act unfaithfully. It is used of Tamar when Judah took her for a harlot (Genesis 38:15) and of Rahab (Joshua 2:1). The brothers’ charge is that Shechem treated their sister as a woman to be bought. Later law would forbid Israel to prostitute a daughter (Leviticus 19:29), and the prophets used the same word for Israel’s spiritual unfaithfulness to God (Hosea 4:12).

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: When a terrible wrong is done to someone we love, what does a faithful response look like?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: Sexual violence is a grievous wrong that God’s people must name and answer with justice and care for the victim, yet neither passive silence nor deceitful vengeance honours God, and the covenant sign must never become a tool of revenge.
discussionQuestions: How does the narrator make clear that Shechem’s act was a serious wrong, and why does it matter that the guilt is placed on him rather than on Dinah?
What might Jacob have done when he first heard the news, and what did his silence communicate to his daughter and his sons?
Why was it wrong for the brothers to use circumcision as a condition they never meant to honour?
How do Hamor’s two speeches (vv. 8-10 and vv. 21-23) differ, and what do they reveal about his aims?
How does Genesis 49:5-7 settle the question the brothers leave hanging in verse 31?
commonMisunderstandings: Dinah is not to blame for what Shechem did to her; the text names him as the one who seized, violated, and defiled her.
The brothers’ final question does not mean the narrator approves the massacre; Jacob’s deathbed curse on their anger gives the verdict.
Shechem’s later affection and generous offer do not erase the crime; he never confesses it and keeps Dinah in his house during the talks.
Circumcision did not make the men of Shechem part of God’s covenant people, because the sign was severed from faith in the God it represented.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Hold together the gravity of the assault, the dignity of the one who was wronged, the failure of the father who stayed silent, and the sin of the brothers who answered evil with deceit and slaughter, while showing that God still preserved this family by grace (35:5).
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Bring every wrong suffered or committed to the God who sees the afflicted, who calls his people to protect the vulnerable, and who has promised to judge justly; leave vengeance with him and follow Christ, who overcame evil with good.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: God’s justice and mercy: he sees and judges evil, forbids his people to take vengeance into their own hands, and offers a true circumcision of the heart through Christ.
flow: Genesis 34 tells honestly of a young woman wronged and a family that failed her in two opposite ways.
God names sexual violence as folly that ought not to be done and keeps company with the brokenhearted.
Human anger, even over a real wrong, turns into sin when it seizes vengeance and uses holy things deceitfully.
Outward religious signs cannot change a heart; God offers a circumcision of the heart by his Spirit.
Christ bore the world’s violence, and those who trust him leave judgment with God and work for justice in his way.
simpleIllustrations: A wedding ring worn to deceive a partner still looks like a ring, but it has been emptied of the promise it was made to carry; so was circumcision in the hands of Jacob’s sons.
A fire set to burn out one weed can sweep across a whole field; anger that will not stop at justice destroys far more than the wrong it meant to punish.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you trust God with the wrongs you have suffered, and let him circumcise your heart so that you answer evil with his justice and mercy rather than your own vengeance?
cautions: Never suggest that a victim of sexual violence brought it on herself; speak of the guilt of the offender and the compassion of God.
Do not use the chapter to justify ethnic hostility or violent religious zeal; the brothers are condemned for exactly that.
Do not reduce the story to a lesson about worldly company; the text’s weight falls on the wrong done to Dinah and on the family’s responses.

reflectionQuestions: When someone near me is wronged, do I tend toward Jacob’s silence or the brothers’ fury, and what would it look like to answer as God does?
Have I ever used something holy, a practice, a promise, or a Bible verse, as a weapon to get my way?
How can I make room for those who have suffered abuse to be heard, believed, and cared for?
Where am I tempted, like Jacob at Shechem, to settle short of what I promised God?
Do I trust that vengeance belongs to God, and that his judgment will be both just and merciful?
